analysis.one_liner: Bars the Education Department from extending COVID-era student loan payment pauses or cancelling balances under emergency powers.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in January 2023 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the Education Department from using its 2003 emergency authority (the HEROES Act) to continue the COVID-era pause on federal student loan payments or to cancel any student loan balances. It would have capped any future emergency payment suspension at 30 days and banned using the emergency authority to wipe out what borrowers owe. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the federal budget and taxpayers generally would have saved the cost of continued payment pauses and cancelled balances, and loan servicers and collection agencies would have resumed a steady stream of payments and collections from borrowers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal budget and loan servicing firms

how_it_helps.text: It would have prohibited the Education Secretary from using the HEROES Act emergency authority in connection with the COVID-19 national emergency declared on March 13, 2020, ending further extensions of the payment moratorium under that authority.
It would have capped any future HEROES-based payment suspension or interest freeze at 30 days, so relief could no longer be extended repeatedly.
It would have barred the Secretary from using the emergency authority to discharge or cancel any outstanding federal student loan balance.

analysis.who_pays: Federal student loan borrowers, who would have had to resume payments and interest accrual and would have lost any path to emergency-based balance cancellation, including the tens of millions affected by the COVID-era pause.

drawbacks.text: Borrowers would have resumed payments and interest accrual immediately upon enactment, adding costs for households still recovering from the pandemic-era economy.

It would have permanently closed the only existing statutory route for broad student debt relief in an emergency, taking that decision away from the executive branch even when a genuine national emergency strikes borrowers.

Supporters argued, in the bill's own findings, that the HEROES Act was meant to help 'affected individuals' such as service members during wars and that blanket moratorium extensions and mass cancellation went beyond what Congress authorized when it passed the law in 2003.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have saved the federal budget real money and reined in a broad reading of emergency authority that the bill's findings call unauthorized. The cost falls entirely on borrowers: resuming payments and interest after a three-year pause, with no emergency-based cancellation of any kind. The trade-off is a genuine one between fiscal restraint and household relief, but the bill was designed as a one-sided cutoff with no alternative relief for borrowers, and it never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Good introduced the Federal Student Loan Integrity Act on January 17, 2023, with four cosponsors, all Republicans.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it.

The bill's findings accused the Education Secretary of exceeding the intent of the 2003 HEROES Act by extending the COVID payment moratorium to borrowers beyond those the law deemed 'affected individuals.'
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still stuck in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal student loan borrowers, who were never hit with the bill's cutoff of payment pauses and balance cancellation. Beyond that, the fight over emergency student debt relief moved to the courts rather than this bill, so its sponsors did not get the statutory rollback they sought.

for.name: Rep. Bob Good
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 17, 2023, to bar further use of the HEROES Act for COVID-era loan relief and cap future emergency payment suspensions.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or vote after it was referred to her committee, leaving it to die there.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were House Republicans (the sponsor plus four cosponsors); no Democrat backed the bill, and with no votes ever taken the partisan shape comes from sponsorship alone.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers and debt collection agencies
industries.note: The bill would have required borrowers to resume payments and interest accrual and barred balance cancellation, restoring the stream of payments and collections these firms process. Borrowers would bear the cost directly.
Ending the moratorium and blocking cancellation would have reduced federal student loan program costs, shifting those costs onto individual borrowers as resumed payments and unpaid balances.

industries.industry: Higher education institutions and borrowers' financial standing
industries.note: Borrowers who would have resumed payments and interest with no relief channel would have had less money for household spending, including loan repayment; the bill offered no offsetting benefit to them.
